case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), the Oklahoma court’s admission/use of highly prejudicial evidence can be reviewed as contrary to or an unreasonable application of “clearly established Federal law” based on Payne’s due-process ‘fundamental unfairness’ principle (as clarified by Carr), or whether no Supreme Court holding clearly establishes that rule outside the victim-impact context.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA deference; ‘clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court of the United States’), applied through the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause’s ‘fundamental fairness’ limitation on unduly prejudicial evidence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Andrew argues the Tenth Circuit defined ‘clearly established Federal law’ too narrowly by demanding a Supreme Court case with closely matching facts and by treating Payne’s due-process holding as limited to victim-impact evidence. In her view, Payne announced a governing constitutional principle—evidence that is ‘so unduly prejudicial that it renders the trial fundamentally unfair’ violates due process—that is sufficiently ‘clearly established’ for AEDPA purposes and applies beyond victim-impact statements. She further contends Carr v. Saul (and other post-Payne decisions) confirm that Payne’s due-process rule is a holding capable of governing related prejudice/fundamental-unfairness claims, so the state court’s contrary approach should be reviewable (and reversible) under § 2254(d)(1).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Warden argues there is no ‘clearly established’ Supreme Court law that squarely governs Andrew’s evidentiary due-process theory in the specific context presented, so § 2254(d)(1) bars relief. Relying on cases like Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall, the respondent emphasizes that habeas courts may not ‘extend’ Supreme Court rationales into new contexts; if the Supreme Court has not expressly applied a rule to the situation at hand, it is not clearly established. The respondent also contends Andrew’s approach would dilute AEDPA’s limits (including exhaustion and the requirement to evaluate the case as presented to the state courts) and invites the federal court to consider arguments or expansions not properly before the state court.
key_precedents: Wright v. Van Patten, 552 U.S. 120 (2008) (per curiam)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument is that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language supplies a generally applicable due-process rule for unduly prejudicial evidence, but as Justice Kagan underscores, Musladin and Woodall prohibit treating broad fairness formulations as “clearly established” law when applying them here would require an extension into a materially different evidentiary context. Justice Thomas’s reminder, grounded in Greene v. Fisher, that § 2254(d)(1) looks only to this Court’s holdings existing at the time of the state decision forecloses any effort to rely on later decisions like Carr v. Saul to fill the gap. Given AEDPA’s constraint, even if the evidence seems troubling on de novo review, it is not unreasonable for the state court to decline to apply a rule we have not squarely held governs this setting. A narrow AEDPA holding best preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding a constitutional pronouncement we lack authority to make on habeas.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument is that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language supplies a generally applicable due-process ceiling on prejudicial evidence, but that contention fails under AEDPA’s text and our cases requiring a holding that squarely governs the specific context. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall prohibit habeas courts from extending broad fairness formulations into a new evidentiary setting to create “clearly established” law under § 2254(d)(1). Justice Kagan’s reliance on Greene v. Fisher further confirms that later-decided cases like Carr cannot retroactively expand the holdings available to assess the reasonableness of the OCCA’s decision. Absent an on-point Supreme Court holding existing at the time of the state adjudication, Oklahoma’s decision cannot be deemed an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law, whatever one thinks of the evidence on de novo review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best shot is to treat Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language as a generally applicable due-process holding limiting highly prejudicial evidence, but that asks us to convert broad language from a distinct victim-impact context into a governing rule for ordinary evidentiary rulings on habeas. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall forbid that kind of extension under § 2254(d)(1) absent a Supreme Court holding squarely on point. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Greene v. Fisher further answers any attempt to lean on Carr v. Saul: it post-dates the OCCA decision and cannot retroactively supply “clearly established” law, and in any event it does not provide a context-specific holding controlling here. On AEDPA’s text, the lack of an on-point holding means Oklahoma’s decision cannot be deemed an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law, whatever one thinks of the evidence on de novo review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best shot is to treat Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language as a generally governing due-process rule that bars evidence so inflammatory it poisons the trial, and that framing resonates with my concern for the real-world effects of prejudicial proof on defendants—especially those least able to protect themselves. But Justice Kagan’s reliance on Musladin and Woodall is hard to escape under AEDPA: using Payne to control an ordinary evidentiary ruling would require the very kind of extension § 2254(d)(1) forbids absent a holding squarely in this context. I also agree with the Chief and Justice Thomas that Greene v. Fisher forecloses using later cases like Carr v. Saul to backfill “clearly established” law at the time the OCCA ruled. On de novo review I might view the admission as constitutionally troubling, but given the statutory limits on federal habeas, I cannot call the state court’s adjudication an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court holdings.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best move is still to treat Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language as a generally applicable due-process holding governing prejudicial evidence, but that asks us to convert broad fairness rhetoric into a context-transcending rule in a setting our holdings have not squarely addressed. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Musladin and Woodall make clear that under § 2254(d)(1) habeas relief cannot rest on extending a general principle into a materially different evidentiary context, even if the extension seems reasonable on de novo review. Justice Barrett’s point about Greene v. Fisher is also decisive for petitioner’s reliance on later clarification (Carr): AEDPA fixes “clearly established” law at the time of the state decision, so later cases cannot backfill the missing on-point holding. Given those constraints, Oklahoma’s adjudication may be debatable as a matter of trial fairness, but it is not an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court holdings.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language could be read as a generally applicable due-process rule against unduly prejudicial evidence, but AEDPA asks for a holding that squarely governs this materially similar context. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall prevent us from converting broad fairness formulations (especially from a distinct victim-impact setting) into “clearly established” law for ordinary evidentiary rulings—granting relief here would necessarily be an extension § 2254(d)(1) forbids. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Greene v. Fisher also matters: later cases like Carr cannot retroactively supply the governing rule or expand the clearly established universe at the time of the OCCA decision. Even if the evidence was troubling, the separation-of-powers choice Congress made in AEDPA cabins habeas to enforcing existing holdings, not announcing new constitutional evidentiary constraints case by case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language sounds like a general due-process constraint on prejudicial evidence, but as the Chief Justice explains, Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall caution that AEDPA does not allow us to treat broad formulations as “clearly established” when applying them would require an extension into a materially different evidentiary context. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Greene v. Fisher reinforces that § 2254(d)(1) is fixed to this Court’s holdings as of the state-court decision, so Carr v. Saul cannot retroactively supply the on-point holding petitioner needs. Even assuming the evidence was troubling on de novo review, under our institutional role and AEDPA’s constraints it is not unreasonable for the state court to decline to apply a Supreme Court rule we have never squarely announced for this category of evidence. I therefore maintain my vote for respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language could be read as a general due-process constraint on unduly prejudicial evidence, but under § 2254(d)(1) that only matters if it is a holding that clearly governs this materially different evidentiary setting. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall preclude habeas courts from converting broad fairness formulations into a new, context-free evidentiary rule—doing so would be an impermissible “extension” rather than application of clearly established law. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Greene v. Fisher also answers petitioner’s Carr v. Saul move: clearly established law is fixed at the time of the state-court decision and is limited to this Court’s holdings, so later clarification cannot supply the missing on-point rule. On this record, even if Oklahoma’s evidentiary ruling is contestable, it is not contrary to or an unreasonable application of any Supreme Court holding squarely addressing this scenario.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best move is still to treat Payne’s “fundamentally unfair” formulation as a generally applicable due-process limit on inflammatory proof, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Musladin and Woodall caution us against converting broad fairness language into “clearly established” law for a materially different evidentiary context on habeas. Justice Kagan’s point about Greene v. Fisher also matters: even if Carr v. Saul underscores that Payne’s due-process language has operative meaning, it cannot retroactively supply clearly established law for the OCCA’s decision, nor does it provide an on-point holding for ordinary evidentiary rulings. Given AEDPA’s constraint, the practical unfairness concerns I share do not permit labeling Oklahoma’s adjudication an unreasonable application of this Court’s holdings. I therefore remain with the respondent notwithstanding the troubling real-world consequences of highly prejudicial evidence.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), relief is available only if the state court’s decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of this Court’s holdings—not dicta—existing at the time of the state-court adjudication. Williams v. Taylor and Greene v. Fisher require that frame, and Carey v. Musladin, Wright v. Van Patten, and White v. Woodall instruct that where this Court has not “squarely address[ed]” the specific context, a habeas court may not extend a general due-process rationale to create “clearly established” law. Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language arose in the victim-impact setting and has not been expressly applied by this Court to the kind of ordinary evidentiary ruling at issue here, so deeming the Oklahoma court unreasonable would require precisely the forbidden extension. Carr v. Saul cannot supply the needed clearly established rule for § 2254(d)(1) purposes, and in any event post-dates the relevant state decision under Greene.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) permits relief only when the state court’s decision is contrary to or an unreasonable application of “clearly established Federal law, as determined by” this Court’s holdings, not general dicta or an extension of reasoning into a new context. Williams v. Taylor defines “clearly established” as this Court’s holdings, and Carey v. Musladin, Wright v. Van Patten, and White v. Woodall reiterate that where no Supreme Court decision squarely governs the specific evidentiary scenario, a habeas court may not extend a due-process ‘fundamental unfairness’ rationale to supply the missing rule. Payne’s discussion of undue prejudice and ‘fundamental unfairness’ arose in the victim-impact context and does not clearly establish a governing rule for this different evidentiary setting as required by Greene v. Fisher’s time-of-decision limitation. Carr v. Saul cannot expand what counts as “clearly established” for § 2254(d)(1) because AEDPA locks the inquiry to prior Supreme Court holdings applicable to the case at hand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), relief is available only if the state court’s decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court holdings, not generalized due-process dicta. Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language arose in the victim-impact context and does not “squarely address” ordinary evidentiary rulings of the sort at issue here, and habeas courts may not extend Supreme Court rationales into new contexts. Carey v. Musladin, 549 U.S. 70 (2006), together with Van Patten and White v. Woodall, confirms that where the Court has not expressly applied a due-process rule to the specific situation, the law is not clearly established for § 2254(d)(1) purposes. Carr v. Saul cannot expand what was clearly established at the time of the OCCA decision (see Greene v. Fisher), and in any event does not supply a holding governing this evidentiary claim on habeas.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) confines habeas relief to state decisions contrary to or unreasonably applying clearly established Supreme Court holdings, not broad constitutional "principles" untethered to a governing holding in the relevant context. Under Carey v. Musladin and White v. Woodall, where this Court has not squarely applied a due-process "fundamental unfairness" rule to the particular kind of evidentiary prejudice alleged, a federal court may not "extend" general fairness language to create clearly established law. Payne’s statement that evidence may violate due process if it renders a trial fundamentally unfair arose in the victim-impact setting, and Carr v. Saul does not transform that context-bound holding into a generally governing evidentiary-due-process rule for § 2254(d)(1) purposes, especially given Greene v. Fisher’s timing limit on what counts as clearly established law. Whatever the troubling real-world effects of the evidence here, § 2254(d)(1) bars relief absent a Supreme Court holding that clearly governs this non-victim-impact evidentiary claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) permits relief only if the state court unreasonably applied a rule that is "clearly established" in this Court’s holdings as of the time of the state decision. While Payne contains broad language about due process and "fundamental unfairness," Musladin and Van Patten instruct that habeas courts may not treat such general formulations as clearly establishing a rule for materially different contexts when this Court has not itself applied the principle there, and Woodall reiterates that § 2254(d)(1) bars "extension" of precedents. Carr may confirm that Payne’s due-process discussion is not mere aside, but under Greene v. Fisher it cannot expand what was clearly established at the relevant time, and in any event it does not supply a holding squarely governing this non-victim-impact evidentiary setting. Given those constraints, Oklahoma’s decision cannot be deemed contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) authorizes relief only when the state court’s decision is contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court,” meaning this Court’s holdings—not dicta—as of the time of the state decision. Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language does not clearly establish a general due-process rule governing the admission of prejudicial evidence outside the victim-impact setting, and § 2254(d)(1) forbids lower federal courts from extending Supreme Court reasoning into new contexts. Carey v. Musladin, Wright v. Van Patten, and White v. Woodall instruct that where our cases have not “squarely addressed” the specific context, there is no clearly established law for habeas purposes, and a state court cannot be deemed unreasonable for declining to apply a rule we have not held applicable. Carr v. Saul cannot supply “clearly established” law for AEDPA because Greene v. Fisher limits that inquiry to Supreme Court holdings existing at the time of the state-court adjudication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), “clearly established Federal law” is limited to this Court’s holdings, not broad dicta, as of the time of the state-court decision. See Williams v. Taylor and Greene v. Fisher. Payne’s statement that evidence may violate due process if it renders a trial “fundamentally unfair” was made in the victim-impact context and has not been squarely applied by this Court to the different evidentiary setting presented here, so granting relief would require extending a rationale into a new context—something Musladin, Van Patten, and White v. Woodall prohibit. Carr v. Saul does not alter the § 2254(d)(1) inquiry because it cannot retroactively supply “clearly established” law for the Oklahoma court’s decision and, in any event, does not constitute a holding applying Payne to ordinary state evidentiary rulings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), “clearly established Federal law” means the holdings of this Court, not broad dicta or general formulations untethered to a holding governing the context at issue. Although Payne v. Tennessee contains language about due process and “fundamental unfairness,” this Court has repeatedly held that habeas relief is unavailable where the petitioner must “extend a rationale” from one context to another because no decision “squarely address[es]” the specific claim (Carey v. Musladin; Wright v. Van Patten; White v. Woodall). Carr v. Saul cannot supply or expand clearly established law for AEDPA purposes, and in any event § 2254(d)(1) looks to Supreme Court holdings as of the time of the state-court decision (Greene v. Fisher). Given those constraints, the Oklahoma court’s evidentiary ruling cannot be deemed contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under AEDPA § 2254(d)(1), “clearly established Federal law” is limited to this Court’s holdings as of the time of the relevant state-court decision, not broad dicta or later elaborations. Payne’s statement that evidence may violate due process when it is “so unduly prejudicial that it renders the trial fundamentally unfair” arose in the victim-impact context and has not been expressly applied by this Court to ordinary evidentiary rulings of the kind at issue here, so granting relief would require extending a rationale into a new context—something Musladin, Van Patten, and Woodall forbid under § 2254(d)(1). Carr v. Saul cannot supply “clearly established” law for AEDPA purposes because Greene v. Fisher confines the inquiry to Supreme Court law existing when the state court ruled. Given those constraints, the Oklahoma court’s decision cannot be deemed “contrary to” or an “unreasonable application” of clearly established law within the meaning of § 2254(d)(1), even if the evidence was highly prejudicial.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the Oklahoma court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court due-process law by allowing evidence/argument so unduly prejudicial that it rendered Brenda Andrew’s capital trial fundamentally unfair, and whether the Tenth Circuit used an impermissibly narrow definition of “clearly established Federal law” to reject that claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA: “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court of the United States”); Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (fundamental fairness limitation on prejudicial evidence).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Andrew argues the Tenth Circuit wrongly refused to recognize a clearly established Supreme Court rule that due process is violated when the State introduces evidence/argument so unduly prejudicial that it makes the trial fundamentally unfair. She contends Payne v. Tennessee articulated that governing principle (not limited to victim-impact evidence), and later cases (including Carr) confirm its status as clearly established. By demanding an overly “on point” Supreme Court case and treating the Payne due-process principle as context-bound dicta, the Tenth Circuit misapplied Williams/Lockyer’s instruction that “clearly established” law includes governing legal principles, even if stated as a generalized standard.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Warden argues AEDPA bars relief because no Supreme Court holding clearly establishes the specific evidentiary limitation Andrew seeks outside the victim-impact context, and habeas courts may not extend Supreme Court rationales to new factual settings (White v. Woodall; Yarborough). The respondent also emphasizes AEDPA constraints such as exhaustion and limiting review to the case presented to the state court (Pinholster; Dunn v. Reeves; Beaudreaux), and contends the Tenth Circuit correctly required a Supreme Court decision that “squarely addresses” the issue rather than a generalized due-process formulation.
key_precedents: Carr v. (Supreme Court capital sentencing case referenced as validating Payne’s due-process principle)
Wright v. Van Patten, 552 U.S. 120 (2008) (per curiam)
Mays v. Hines / Beaudreaux v. Cain, 585 U.S. 961 (2018) (cited for AEDPA error-correction principles)
Davis v. Straub, 430 F.3d 281 (6th Cir. 2005) (Merritt, J., dissenting)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: Williams and Lockyer allow clearly established law to be stated at a general level, and Yarborough’s “fairminded disagreement” rubric typically operates at the application step. But Musladin and Woodall still draw the AEDPA line where the habeas claim depends on treating broad “fundamental unfairness” language—especially language not necessary to the specific holding—as a controlling rule in a distinct prejudicial-evidence/argument setting; that is an extension, not an application, and fairminded jurists can disagree about its reach here. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Carr does not move the § 2254(d)(1) inquiry because later reiterations cannot supply clearly established law as of the state-court decision, nor can they transform nonessential generalities into a governing holding that squarely controls. On that understanding, the Tenth Circuit’s approach is not an impermissibly cramped definition of clearly established law but a faithful application of our repeated warnings against converting general due-process formulations into habeas commands.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor argue that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” language is itself a clearly established governing principle, so applying it here is not an impermissible extension. But under AEDPA as we applied it in Musladin and Woodall, a habeas court may not convert broad due-process verbiage—especially outside a holding squarely addressing this evidentiary/argument context—into a rule that dictates relief; doing so necessarily extends precedent rather than applies it. Even if Payne is read to announce a general fairness ceiling, Yarborough and Lockyer confirm that such general standards leave substantial room for fairminded disagreement, so Oklahoma’s rejection cannot be deemed objectively unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1). Justice Jackson’s reliance on Carr does not change that, because clearly established law is fixed at the time of the state-court decision and later reiterations cannot supply the missing governing holding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor most forcefully argue that Williams/Lockyer allow clearly established law to be stated as a general principle and that Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” backstop supplies that principle across contexts, leaving only the Yarborough reasonableness inquiry. But Musladin and Woodall are precisely about why that move fails under AEDPA when the purported rule is broad, context-bound due-process phrasing not necessary to a holding that squarely addresses this materially different evidentiary/trial-atmosphere scenario; treating Payne’s caveat as controlling here effectively extends precedent. Even if one accepts Kagan’s framing that a general ceiling exists, Yarborough confirms that such open-ended standards create wide latitude for “fairminded disagreement,” and Oklahoma’s rejection therefore cannot be labeled objectively unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1). Justice Jackson’s reliance on Carr does not alter the analysis because later decisions cannot retroactively supply “clearly established” law or convert nonessential language into a governing holding as of the state-court decision.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Musladin/Woodall argument is the most serious, but I continue to think it mislocates where those cases bite: they constrain granting relief by extending precedent at step two (objective unreasonableness), not by redefining step one so narrowly that Payne’s due-process backstop ceases to be “clearly established” outside victim-impact evidence. As Justice Kagan notes, Williams and Lockyer allow clearly established law to be articulated as a general governing principle, and Payne’s “fundamental unfairness” ceiling operates as the constitutional limiter that makes the underlying admissibility rule lawful rather than a context-bound aside. Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett are right that Yarborough leaves room for fairminded disagreement, but that is an argument about whether Oklahoma’s application was reasonable—not a license to demand a fact-matched holding before the fairness constraint exists at all, especially in capital sentencing where real-world prejudice can distort life-or-death judgment. Carr (raised by Justice Jackson) cannot supply clearly established law retroactively, but it does underscore that our doctrine has long treated fundamental fairness as a cross-context due-process limitation, reinforcing that the state court had a governing standard to apply.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Musladin/Woodall argument is the strongest, but I think it mislocates the extension problem: those cases prevent habeas courts from crafting a new constitutional rule, not from recognizing that Payne itself (as reaffirmed alongside its approval of victim-impact evidence) preserves a due-process ceiling against evidence or argument that renders a proceeding fundamentally unfair. As Justice Barrett notes, some language in Payne may not have been essential, but the “fundamental unfairness” backstop is not free-floating dicta—it is the constitutional limitation that makes the holding coherent, and Williams/Lockyer permit clearly established law to be a general governing standard. Yarborough’s “room for fairminded disagreement,” emphasized by Justices Kavanaugh and Roberts, properly operates at step two (objective unreasonableness), not by redefining step one so narrowly that the due-process ceiling becomes unavailable absent a fact-matched Supreme Court case. On a pragmatic textualist reading of § 2254(d)(1), the question is whether Oklahoma unreasonably applied that general standard on these facts, not whether the standard exists.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Williams and Lockyer allow “clearly established” law to be stated at a higher level of generality and that Payne includes a due-process “fundamental unfairness” backstop. But Musladin and Woodall still control the AEDPA question here: converting Payne’s generalized, context-bound unfairness caveat—especially language not necessary to its holding—into a dispositive rule for a materially different prejudicial-evidence/argument scenario is precisely the sort of precedent “extension” § 2254(d)(1) forbids. And even if Payne’s language is treated as a governing principle, Yarborough and Lockyer underscore that such open-ended standards leave room for fairminded disagreement, which defeats any claim that Oklahoma’s decision was objectively unreasonable. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Carr does not change my view because AEDPA fixes “clearly established Federal law” at the time of the state-court decision and later reiterations cannot retroactively supply a missing controlling holding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the best point that Williams and Lockyer allow clearly established law to be framed at some generality, and that the “room for disagreement” language in Yarborough is usually about unreasonable application. But Musladin and Woodall still require a Supreme Court holding that actually governs the type of claim presented, and I do not think Payne’s generalized due-process backstop—stated in the course of approving victim-impact evidence—can be treated as controlling law for this distinct prejudicial-evidence/argument scenario without effectively extending precedent under AEDPA, as Chief Justice Roberts argues. Even if Payne supplies a general fairness ceiling, Yarborough and Lockyer confirm that such an open-ended standard leaves enough space for fairminded disagreement that Oklahoma’s decision cannot be labeled objectively unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1). On an institutional, precedent-bound view of AEDPA, the Tenth Circuit’s approach is not impermissibly cramped; it reflects our repeated instruction not to convert broad fairness formulations into dispositive habeas rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Williams and Lockyer allow clearly established law to be articulated as a general governing principle, and that Yarborough’s “fairminded disagreement” typically bears on application rather than definition. But Musladin and Woodall still constrain us from treating broad due-process “fundamental unfairness” language—especially language not necessary to resolve the specific evidentiary context in Payne—as a controlling holding for a materially different prejudicial-argument scenario; doing so effectively extends precedent under § 2254(d)(1). Even if one accepts Justice Sotomayor’s concern that narrowing Payne risks hollowing out the due-process backstop, Yarborough and Lockyer underscore that such open-ended standards leave enough discretion that Oklahoma’s decision cannot be deemed objectively unreasonable on habeas. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Carr does not alter the AEDPA inquiry because clearly established law is fixed at the time of the state-court decision and later reiterations cannot supply a missing, context-controlling holding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Musladin/Woodall objection is the strongest: AEDPA does not allow habeas courts to "extend" our precedents by converting broad due-process language into a new rule. But I remain persuaded, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, that the Tenth Circuit’s approach improperly collapses the two steps by defining “clearly established” law so narrowly that Payne’s constitutional backstop—due process prohibits evidence/argument so unduly prejudicial it renders the proceeding fundamentally unfair—ceases to function as any governing standard outside victim-impact evidence, which Williams and Lockyer reject. Musladin and Woodall police invention of new, context-specific rules from dicta; they do not require near fact-identity when a holding supplies a general governing principle, and Yarborough’s “fairminded disagreement” properly belongs in assessing whether Oklahoma’s application was objectively unreasonable, not in erasing the governing ceiling at the threshold. On a progressive-pragmatist view attentive to capital sentencing consequences, I cannot endorse an AEDPA methodology that makes fundamental-fairness review effectively unavailable for extreme prejudicial appeals simply because the prejudice arises in a different evidentiary posture than Payne’s facts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), we may grant relief only if the state court unreasonably applied clearly established law as determined by this Court’s holdings, not generalized notions untethered to a specific holding. Carey v. Musladin and White v. Woodall caution that where our precedents have not squarely addressed the particular evidentiary or trial-atmosphere claim, a federal habeas court may not treat broad due-process language (including in Payne) as "clearly established" law and then extend it to a new context. Even assuming a general “fundamental fairness” principle exists, Yarborough v. Alvarado and Lockyer v. Andrade teach that such general standards leave room for fairminded disagreement, which AEDPA requires us to respect. Given those constraints and the interest in institutional legitimacy, I would not disturb Oklahoma’s judgment on the theory that the Tenth Circuit applied an impermissibly narrow definition of clearly established law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under AEDPA, relief is available only if the state court’s decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court,” meaning this Court’s holdings—not generalized dicta about “fundamental fairness.” 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor. Decisions like Carey v. Musladin and White v. Woodall forbid granting habeas relief where the petitioner must extend a Supreme Court rationale to a new context; Payne’s due-process language, largely stated in the victim-impact setting, does not clearly establish a holding governing the distinct evidentiary/argument issues pressed here. Given that constraint, the Oklahoma court’s adjudication cannot be deemed an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established law, and the Tenth Circuit did not err by requiring a Supreme Court decision that squarely addresses the claimed constitutional rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is unavailable unless the state court unreasonably applied a Supreme Court holding that clearly governs the claim, and AEDPA does not permit extending this Court’s rationales to new factual settings. Carey v. Musladin and White v. Woodall make clear that generalized “fundamental fairness” language, or principles stated outside a controlling holding, do not constitute clearly established law for § 2254(d)(1) purposes when our decisions have not squarely addressed the specific type of prejudicial evidence or courtroom influence at issue. Payne’s discussion of due-process limits arose in the victim-impact context, and whatever broader language it contains does not supply a clearly established rule compelling relief here, especially given Yarborough v. Alvarado’s instruction that broad standards leave substantial room for reasonable disagreement. Because the Oklahoma court could reasonably reject the due-process claim under existing holdings, the Tenth Circuit did not err in denying relief.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) requires deference, but it does not permit a federal court to define “clearly established Federal law” so narrowly that only a fact-matched Supreme Court case counts; Williams v. Taylor and Lockyer v. Andrade recognize that clearly established law includes governing legal principles stated at an appropriate level of generality. Payne v. Tennessee expressly articulated the Due Process limitation that the State may not introduce evidence or argument so “unduly prejudicial” that it “renders the trial fundamentally unfair,” and this Court later reiterated that principle in Carr, confirming it as a constitutional rule not confined to a victim-impact silo. If the Oklahoma court allowed a prejudicial evidentiary presentation that crossed that fundamental-fairness line, treating Payne’s rule as non-existent outside victim-impact evidence is an unreasonable application of clearly established due-process law under § 2254(d)(1), not a mere refusal to extend precedent under Woodall/Yarborough. Given the capital context and the risk of verdict distortion, the Tenth Circuit’s approach threatens to strip vulnerable defendants of the minimal due-process backstop that Payne and the Fourteenth Amendment require.
